candidate_sources.title: Anthracnose Fruit Rot (Ripe Rot) of Blueberries | NC State Extension Publications
candidate_sources.snippet: Anthracnose fruit rot, also called ripe rot, is caused by Colletotrichum acutatum and C. gloeosporioides. Blossom infections remain symptomless until fruit ripen, then develop sunken lesions and orange to salmon-colored spore masses. The fungus overwinters in infected twigs, bud scales, and fruit spurs. Management includes fungicides from bloom through harvest, prompt harvest, and rapid cooling.

candidate_sources.title: FS1361: Anthracnose Fruit Rot in Highbush Blueberry (Rutgers NJAES)
candidate_sources.snippet: Anthracnose fruit rot in highbush blueberry is caused by Colletotrichum species. Infection can occur from bloom but stays dormant until fruit fully ripen (ripe rot). Symptoms include sunken lesions, softening, and viscous yellow to orange conidia. Management covers irrigation timing, fungicide programs, harvest practices, and cultivar selection.

candidate_sources.title: Michigan Blueberry Facts: Anthracnose Fruit Rot (Ripe Rot) - Michigan State University
candidate_sources.snippet: Anthracnose fruit rot, caused by Colletotrichum acutatum, is the most common and widespread fruit disease of blueberries. Called ripe rot because blossom infections remain symptomless until fruit ripen, then shrivel with sunken lesions and orange/salmon spore masses. The fungus overwinters in dead twigs, bud scales, and fruit spurs; floral bud scales are the most important inoculum source. Preharvest losses of 10-20% and postharvest losses up to 100% reported.

candidate_sources.title: Blueberry IPM - Anthracnose Ripe Rot | UMass Amherst Center for Agriculture
candidate_sources.snippet: Anthracnose ripe rot of blueberry is caused by Colletotrichum acutatum and C. gloeosporioides. Leaf spot symptoms include circular brown spots with concentric bulls-eye rings; fruit develop sunken lesions and salmon spore masses. At 25C, at least 8 hours of leaf wetness is required for infection. Management includes irrigation timing and fungicide sprays from bloom through harvest.

candidate_sources.title: Fruit Rots of Blueberry: Alternaria, Anthracnose, and Botrytis | Ohioline (Ohio State University)
candidate_sources.snippet: Anthracnose fruit rot of blueberry is caused by Colletotrichum acutatum. Infection occurs at bloom but symptoms appear at ripening, with soft rotted fruit and orange spore masses at the blossom end. Covers symptoms, disease cycle, and management alongside Alternaria and Botrytis fruit rots.

candidate_sources.title: PP385/PP385: Leaf Rust Disease of Southern Highbush Blueberry in Florida
candidate_sources.snippet: In Florida, the fungus Thekopsora minima causes leaf rust on southern highbush blueberry. Symptoms on the upper leaf surface appear as subcircular to angular chlorotic spots that develop necrotic reddish to brown centers with reddish purple margins; orange to yellow uredinia appear on the lower leaf surface. Infected bushes can show premature defoliation, decreased floral bud differentiation, and reduced yield.

candidate_sources.title: Blueberry Leaf Rust | Ohioline (Ohio State University Extension)
candidate_sources.snippet: Blueberry leaf rust caused by Pucciniastrum vaccinii first appears as yellow leaf spots on the upper surface of new leaves that later turn reddish brown; yellowish-orange pustules become visible on the lower leaf surface. Severe infections cause premature defoliation. Management includes removing hemlocks (the alternate host), growing less susceptible cultivars, and fungicide applications.

candidate_sources.title: Leaf Rust of Blueberry â€“ Blueberries (eXtension)
candidate_sources.snippet: Leaf rust of blueberry produces yellow spots on the upper leaf surface that turn reddish brown, with yellowish orange pustules on the lower leaf surface by mid-summer. Mild temperatures (65â€“68Â°F) and multiple days of rain are conducive to infection. Rabbiteye cultivars suffer premature defoliation; highbush blueberries are subject to localized outbreaks in eastern coastal states. Management includes hemlock removal, cultural controls, and fungicides.

candidate_sources.title: Blueberry (Vaccinium corymbosum)-Rust | Pacific Northwest Pest Management Handbooks
candidate_sources.snippet: Rust of blueberry (Vaccinium corymbosum) caused by Thekopsora minima (syn. Pucciniastrum vaccinii / Naohidemyces vaccinii). Provides symptom descriptions, disease cycle involving the hemlock alternate host, and cultural and chemical management recommendations.

candidate_sources.title: Phomopsis Twig Blight of Blueberry | Ohioline
candidate_sources.snippet: Phomopsis twig blight, caused by the fungus Phomopsis vaccinii (sexual stage Diaporthe vaccinii), is a common disease of highbush blueberry. The fungus overwinters in infected canes and twigs; in spring spores are dispersed from pycnidia by rain. Infected buds become brown and die, a necrotic brown lesion forms on the twig, and stems wilt with premature red/brown leaf color. Management includes removing and burning blighted wood during dormant pruning.

candidate_sources.title: Phomopsis Canker and Twig Blight in Blueberries in Home Fruit Plantings
candidate_sources.snippet: A typical symptom is sudden wilting and death (flagging) of canes during the growing season, with a sunken or flattened canker often present at the base of the cane. The fungus enters young floral parts before and during bloom causing twig blight, and also enters through wounds to infect young cane tips and cause cankers that move into the stem. Remove and burn blighted wood; avoid plant injury and drought stress.

candidate_sources.title: Phomopsis vaccinii (Phomopsis twig blight of blueberry) | CABI Plantwise Plus Knowledge Bank
candidate_sources.snippet: Phomopsis twig and blossom blight, canker and dieback is caused by the fungus Phomopsis vaccinii (sexual stage Diaporthe vaccinii) and is a common disease of highbush blueberry. Infected twigs turn brown to dark brown; blossoms become blighted and shriveled. Cankers are elongated, flattened areas covered with pinpoint-sized pycnidia. The disease can severely decrease yields on susceptible varieties.

candidate_sources.title: Twig Blight of Blueberry | NC State Extension Publications
candidate_sources.snippet: Twig blight of blueberry caused by Phomopsis vaccinii (Diaporthe vaccinii). Brown, spreading lesions develop on green stems and twigs, which are eventually killed. Infected stems wilt during summer and leaves turn color earlier, causing red flagging. The fungus overwinters in infected plant debris and spores are spread by rain splash; infection occurs through flower buds from budbreak to bloom.

candidate_sources.title: Mummy Berry Disease of Blueberry | NC State Extension Publications
candidate_sources.snippet: Mummy berry is caused by the fungus Monilinia vaccinii-corymbosi. The disease has two infection phases: a shoot/leaf blight phase where leaves wilt and form a shepherd's crook, and a fruit infection phase where berries become tan, then gray, shriveled, hard mummies. The fungus is windborne; mummified berries overwinter on the ground and are the source of infection the following year. Management includes raking, cultivating, mulching to bury mummies, and fungicides.

candidate_sources.title: Mummy Berry of Blueberry Caused by Monilinia vaccinii-corymbosi: A Diagnostic Guide | Plant Health Progress
candidate_sources.snippet: A diagnostic guide for mummy berry of blueberry caused by Monilinia vaccinii-corymbosi. Covers the shoot blight (shoot strike) phase with browning along major leaf veins and shepherd's crook wilting, and the fruit infection phase where infected green berries reveal white fungal growth in the locules and ripening berries appear pinkish tan, slightly ridged, and rubbery with a gray to black fungal mass inside.

candidate_sources.title: Mummy Berry Facts (E2846) | Michigan State University Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Pathogen: Monilinia vaccinii-corymbosi (Reade) Honey. Mummy berry attacks new growth, blossoms, foliage and fruit and can cause extensive losses. Tips of newly infected leaves, buds, stems, and flower clusters suddenly wilt, turn brown, and become covered with a powdery mass of spores. Infected fruit shrivel into mummies that overwinter on the ground. Control relies on cultural practices and prophylactic fungicide use early in the season.

candidate_sources.title: Blueberry - Phomopsis Canker and Twig Blight - University of Maine Cooperative Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Phomopsis canker and twig blight of blueberry is caused by the fungus Phomopsis vaccinii. Symptoms include 'flagging' where individual stems wilt and die while leaves turn reddish and remain attached, dark brown lesions and death of young twigs, with lesions extending up to several inches from the tip of the twig and possibly more than one lesion per twig.

candidate_sources.title: Phomopsis vaccinii (Phomopsis twig blight of blueberry) | CABI Compendium
candidate_sources.snippet: Twig canker and blight caused by Phomopsis vaccinii (teleomorph Diaporthe vaccinii) is a harmful disease of highbush blueberry and cranberry. Symptoms include dieback and flagging of stems, mottling of stem tissues beneath the bark, browning of pith, blighting of blossoms and twigs, premature coloring of green fruit, and fruit drop.

candidate_sources.title: Blueberry Disease Fast Facts: Canker Diseases | Cornell University
candidate_sources.snippet: There are two significant canker diseases found throughout New York State on highbush blueberries: Phomopsis canker/twig blight and Fusicoccum (Godronia) canker. Each is caused by a fungus; Phomopsis vaccinii and Fusicoccum putrefaciens, respectively. Cankers appear as elongated, flattened areas covered with pinpoint pycnidia.
